title: Spiritually Awake People Slowly Quit These 7 Things (And Never Look Back)
fullText: There is a moment that happens to some people, not all people, but [music] some. It does not arrive with a lightning bolt or a dramatic scene. It does not show up because you read the right book or found the right teacher or had the perfect retreat weekend in the mountains. It just arrives quietly [music] like a window cracking open in a room that has been sealed shut for years. And in [music] that moment, something in you realizes that the life you have been living, the version of yourself you have been performing, the game you have been playing without ever questioning the rules, none of it fits the way it used to. The shoes are too tight. [music] The mask is too heavy. The script you have been reading from feels like someone else wrote it for someone else entirely. That is what some people call a spiritual awakening. And I want to tell you something about that phrase right now because a lot of people hear it and immediately picture someone sitting cross-legged on a mountain with a glowing face and perfect peace. That is not what I am talking about. What I am talking about is something much more ordinary [music] and much more real. Spiritual awakening at its core is simply the process of becoming more honest. More honest about who you actually are. [music] More honest about what you actually want. more honest about what you have been carrying that was never really yours to carry in the first place. [music] And when that process begins, something fascinating happens. You start letting things go, [music] not because you planned to, not because someone told you to, but because you genuinely cannot hold on to them anymore. It is like your hands just slowly, [music] naturally open. Today we are going to talk about seven of those things. [music] seven patterns, habits, and ways of being that people consistently report falling away from as they begin to wake up to their deeper selves. These are not things you decide to quit. [music] They are things that quietly become impossible to continue. If you have been feeling lately like something is shifting in you, [music] like you are becoming someone you do not quite recognize yet, like the things that used to motivate you are losing their grip, then this is for you. Let [music] us begin. One, [clears throat] the hunger to be approved of. The first thing that starts to fall away is one of the [music] most deeply wired patterns most of us carry. The need for other people to tell us we are okay. Think about how early that need gets installed in us. [music] From the time we are children, approval is the currency of survival. [music] You behave the right way. You get a smile. You achieve something. You get praise. [music] You fit in. You get accepted. And rejection, even subtle rejection, feels like a small emergency to the nervous system. So you learn very early to scan the room, to read the temperature, to adjust yourself accordingly. [music] By the time most of us reach adulthood, this has become completely automatic. We shape our opinions based on who is in the room. We soften our edges in certain company. We say yes when we mean no. We laugh at things we do not find [music] funny. We bite our tongues, shrink ourselves, exaggerate the parts of ourselves that seem to land well and hide the parts that might make people uncomfortable. And for a long time, this works, or at least it functions. [music] It keeps the social piece. It keeps us feeling like we belong. But something changes when you start waking up. The approval seeking machinery begins to malfunction. You will be in the middle of a conversation about to say what you think the other person wants to hear, and something inside you just will not let you do it. Not from stubbornness, not from rebellion, something deeper than that. It is more like your body has developed a genuine intolerance. [music] People going through this describe it in strikingly similar ways. One person said it felt like trying to wear a coat that used to fit perfectly [music] but had somehow shrunk three sizes. They kept trying to put it on. It kept not fitting. Eventually, they had to just set it down. [music] That is what quitting the approval hunger actually feels like. You do not announce it. You do not make a speech about authenticity. You just find yourself increasingly unable to perform the old show. Now, this transition is not comfortable. There is a gap period where you have stopped internally needing approval, but have not yet adjusted your external world to match. You might still catch yourself checking how many people liked your post. Still noticing when someone seems disappointed in you. Still feeling a small sting when you do not get the validation you use to chase. But the difference is you notice it now. You see the machinery. [music] You are not fully inside it anymore. And on the other side of that gap, something extraordinary waits. A settled sense of your own worth that does not need external confirmation to stay lit. Not arrogance, not indifference to others. [music] Just a quiet inner knowing that you exist, that you are enough, that your value does not need to be voted on. It is one of the most liberating feelings a human being can experience. and it becomes available when the desperate hunger for approval finally starts to quiet down. Two, [music] the need to stand out as special. The second thing that falls away might surprise you because it sounds like it would be a good thing to keep. The need to be special. Here is the thing. There is an enormous difference between actually being yourself fully and unapologetically and needing to be seen as exceptional. between having genuine depth and needing others to recognize your depth, between being spiritually sincere [music] and needing to be the most spiritually advanced person in the room. What often happens early in a personal awakening [music] is something that looks like growth but is actually just the ego finding a new costume. [music] You have a real insight, a genuine experience, a moment of clarity that feels profound. And then very naturally the ego moves in and says [music] great now let us use this to be special. Suddenly you are subtly mentioning your meditation practice dropping references to consciousness in casual conversations feeling a quiet sense of superiority toward people who have not had your experiences [music] or seen what you have seen. You are not bragging exactly but you are definitely differentiating yourself from what you might privately call the unconscious masses. This phase can last a while. It is a real phase. Most people go through some version of it. But if growth continues, something eventually cracks. You catch yourself mid-sentence. You hear what you are actually saying, [music] and you see it clearly for what it is. You are using your spiritual awakening as a social strategy. [music] You are turning genuine inner experience into external performance. And the moment you see it, you cannot unsee it. One man described the exact moment this happened to him. [music] He was at a dinner party in the middle of explaining something about presence and consciousness to a group of people who had not asked and he said he suddenly felt like he was watching himself from across the room and what he saw looked small insecure. He was using big ideas to make himself feel bigger. He got quiet after that not from embarrassment but from something shifting. He stopped needing people to know how spiritually serious he was. [music] And here is the paradox that people consistently report on the other side of this. When you stop trying to stand out, your actual self naturally emerges. The performance was always covering the real thing. When you quit the performance, what is left is genuinely you. Unpolished, unannounced, and paradoxically far more interesting than the curated version ever was. Being ordinary becomes unexpectedly a [music] relief. Not a defeat, a relief. Three, the performance of constant positivity. [music] Third on this list, and maybe the one that surprises people the most, is the slow quitting of forced happiness. We live in a culture that has a complicated relationship with difficult emotions, especially in spiritual and self-help communities. There is enormous pressure to be positive, to radiate good vibes, to be beyond negativity, [music] to have moved past anger, sadness, fear, grief, to be living proof that your practice is working by never appearing to struggle. [music] This creates a very particular kind of mask. Not the social mask of everyday [music] life, but a spiritually flavored mask. Everything happens for a reason. I am at peace with what is. I choose love. All of which may be genuinely true sometimes. But when these phrases become reflexive shields against actually feeling something, they stop being wisdom and start being armor. [music] As people deepen in their awakening, the armor gets heavier and at some point the weight becomes unbearable. What happens is not a descent into negativity. It is actually the opposite. It is the beginning of genuine emotional honesty. The full spectrum of human experience gets allowed back in. Grief [music] gets to be grief. Anger gets to be anger. Fear gets to be fear. Not forever, not without processing, but without denial. A woman who had been a yoga teacher for 12 years described going through this. She had built her whole identity around being the calm, centered, luminous one. [music] Her students came to her precisely because she seemed so unshakably at peace. [music] Then she went through a divorce and she tried to keep the mask on. [music] She got on her mat. She breathed. She said the right things. And one day in the middle of teaching a class, [music] she just started crying and could not stop. She thought her career was over. What actually happened was that her realness became the teaching. Her students trusted her more after that moment than they ever had before because they could finally feel that she was a human being, [music] not a performance. That is what dropping the positivity performance creates. not more suffering, more connection, more realness, more actual peace as opposed to performed peace. [music] There is a version of okayness that you perform for others and even for yourself. [music] And there is a version of okayness that you have genuinely arrived at after sitting with what is hard. Those are completely different things. And the people who are waking up are slowly learning to tell the difference. Four, the desperate grip uncertainty. The fourth thing that falls away as people awaken is one of the most disorienting losses and also one of the most profound freedoms. The need to be certain. Most of us have built our inner lives on a foundation of things we know. I know who I am. I know what I believe. I know what the right path is. I know what happens when you die. I know why things happen the way they did in my past. [music] I know what kind of person I am deep down. These certainties feel like safety, like the floor beneath your feet. Without them, life seems like it might just swallow you whole. But there is a cost to this certainty that we rarely talk about. When you are certain, you are closed. Your categories are fixed. New information either gets forced into the existing frame or rejected entirely. Your map of reality stays small because you stop questioning it. [music] Awakening has a way of dissolving certainty. Not all at once, gradually. It starts with the small stuff. You realize an opinion you held strongly was actually just something you absorbed from your environment without ever examining. You notice you were wrong about something you were completely sure of. [music] And each small dissolution teaches you that certainty itself might be the problem, not the [music] solution. Then it goes deeper. You find yourself less certain about why things happened in your past. Less certain about other people's [music] motivations, including people you thought you understood completely. less certain about your own identity, about what you really are underneath all the roles and labels and stories. [music] A man who spent decades in academic research described this experience as the most unsettling gift he had ever received. He had built his entire sense of self on being the guy who understood things, the analyst, the expert, the one with answers. [music] And then gradually his intellectual certainty began to feel hollow. Not wrong, exactly. Just then, like he had been studying the menu and calling it a meal, he said something I want to sit with for a moment. He said the less certain he became, the more present he was. Because certainty lives in the past and the [music] future, in what you have figured out and what you have already decided. Presence lives in the open, unresolved, [music] genuinely curious moment. On the other side of lost certainty is something called wonder. The capacity to be genuinely surprised by life, to not already know the answer [music] before the question is finished. To hold two contradictory things at the same time without needing to collapse them [music] into a single verdict. This is not confusion. It is what actual wisdom feels like from the inside. [music] Not the accumulation of answers, but the expansion of the capacity to live inside questions. Five, blame as a way of life. The fifth thing that slowly falls away might be the hardest to release because it feels so justified, so earned. [music] Blame. Not just blaming others in petty everyday ways. The deeper structural habit of organizing your story around what was done to you. Making sense of your pain through the lens of who [music] caused it. Building your identity in part around your wounds and who is responsible for them. And here's the thing. I want to be very careful and very honest here because some things that happened to you were genuinely not your fault. [music] Some of the harm you experienced was real, serious, and caused by real people who made real choices that hurt you. Acknowledging that is important. Sitting with it is important. [music] Processing it honestly is important. What we are talking about is something that comes after that. The moment when the blame which once served to locate the source of pain becomes the cage you live inside. [music] Blame has a seductive logic. It explains everything. It protects your sense of innocence. It gives you a community of people who understand your pain. It provides an identity and it quietly prevents any movement because as long as the problem is entirely located outside yourself, [music] there is nothing you can do to change it. As people go through genuine awakening, they begin to notice something uncomfortable patterns. The same dynamic showing up in relationship after relationship. The same flavor of disappointment, betrayal, [music] or being overlooked, following them through jobs, friendships, and partnerships. The same [music] story with different characters. And eventually comes the question that changes everything. [music] Not why do people keep doing this to me? But what role am I playing in this? not from self-punishment, not from the belief that the harm was deserved, [music] but from a genuine and radical desire to reclaim authorship of your own life. A woman who had spent years carrying real and legitimate pain from her childhood eventually arrived at what she described as the [music] loneliest, most terrifying, and ultimately most liberating realization of her life. She saw how she had organized her entire identity around being the one who was wronged. And she saw clearly [music] and honestly how that identity had become a way of avoiding her own power. [music] She said letting go of blame did not mean letting the people who hurt her off the hook. It meant [music] taking herself off the hook. Off the hook of helplessness. Off the hook of waiting for the people who hurt her to change or apologize or finally understand before she could move forward. [music] The people who release blame do not become naive or passive. They become formidable because they have taken back the pen. [music] They are no longer waiting for someone else to write a different ending to their story. Six, [music] using spirituality as an escape hatch. The sixth pattern that falls away for people who are genuinely growing is a subtle and tricky one. Using spiritual ideas and [music] practices to avoid the actual experience of being human. This one is worth unpacking carefully because it looks so much like growth from the outside. [music] You have gone through something painful, a breakup, a loss, a crisis of identity, [music] and you respond by going deep into your practice. You meditate more. You read everything you can about consciousness and impermanence and the nature of the self. You talk about detachment and acceptance and the illusion of the ego. And on the surface, this looks like wisdom. But sometimes, and this happens to a lot of sincere and intelligent people, the spiritual framework becomes a way of skipping over the experience rather than moving through it. You do not grieve. You philosophize about grief. [music] You do not feel the anger. You reframe it as misplaced energy. [music] You do not sit with the loneliness. You remind yourself that separation is an illusion. This is called spiritual bypassing. And it is one of the most common detours on the path of growth. The giveaway is usually in the [music] body. The feelings you have been refraraming and philosophizing around do not actually go away. They live in the muscles, in the [music] chest, in the tightening throat, in the restless nights. The mind has all the right answers. The body is still keeping score. What genuine awakening eventually demands is full embodiment. Not just the transcendent parts, not just the expanded consciousness and the beautiful insights, the whole thing. The grief and the hunger and the irritability and the longing [music] and the very ordinary very human need to be seen, held and loved. A man who had been practicing meditation seriously for over 15 years came to understand this only after a period of profound personal [music] loss. He had all the tools. He knew how to sit. He knew how to observe. He knew the vocabulary of non-attachment inside and out. And he was falling apart. Not because the practice was wrong, but because he had been using the practice as an elevated form of not showing up for his own pain. He had to learn all over again how to cry, how to [music] want things, how to admit that he was scared, how to need other people. He described it as coming back to Earth after a long time in orbit. disorienting at first, [music] heavier, but also more real than anything he had touched in years. The invitation here is not to abandon the spiritual tools. It is to stop using them as an exit. To let them be what they are at their best, a way [music] deeper into life, not a way around it. Seven, the identity of being the awakened one. The seventh and final pattern that falls away is perhaps the quietest of all and in some ways the most important. The identity of being spiritually awake in a world of sleeping people. Early in awakening, this identity has a certain logic to it. You are seeing things differently [music] than the people around you. You are asking questions they are not asking. You are feeling the emptiness of things they are still chasing and there is a real honest, sometimes painful sense of dislocation that comes with that. You do not fit the way you used to. Some of the conversations that used to feel normal now feel hollow. But there is a crucial fork in the [music] road here. One Direction turns that dislocation into a story about superiority. [music] I am more awake. I see what they cannot see. I have gone somewhere they have not been. This story has a seductive quality because it takes something genuinely disorienting, the feeling of not fitting in anymore, and gives it a flattering explanation. [music] The other direction leads somewhere much more interesting. People who continue to genuinely grow [music] eventually see through this story. They realize that the sense of separation they felt was not evidence of their awakening. It was evidence of their unhealed need to feel above [music] something. That the isolation they mistook for spiritual advancement was actually a kind of fear. Fear of being seen in their humanness, fear of being ordinary, [music] fear of intimacy. And when that layer drops, something remarkable happens. [music] They find they can connect with almost anyone. Not by dumbing themselves down, not by pretending to share values they do not share, but by recognizing their own humanness in every [music] person they encounter, by remembering what it was like to be asleep, by having genuine compassion for people still inside patterns they themselves have only recently started to recognize. [music] A woman who had spent years in what she described as spiritual solitude, carefully guarding her inner world from what she saw as lower vibrations, had a moment of realization on a flight home from a conference. She was sitting next to a man who was talking loudly on his phone, complaining about his boss, stressed about something at work, and she noticed herself judging him, feeling impatient, [music] pulling away. And then something shifted. She looked at him and she saw herself, not the current version of herself, the version from 10 years before, overwhelmed, [music] reactive, not yet knowing what she now knew. And instead of the usual distance, she felt something open up in her chest. [music] Warmth, recognition, a kind of love that did not require him to be different. That is what genuine awakening looks like. Not separation, deeper [music] and more honest connection. Not finding your tribe of enlightened ones and retreating there. Meeting people where they actually are, including where you yourself still are, [music] which is beautifully and permanently human. So there they are. Seven things that quietly fall away as you begin to wake up to your actual life. The desperate hunger for approval. The need to be special and seen as spiritually exceptional. The performance of constant positivity. the grip on certainty, [music] blame as an organizing principle, spiritual bypassing, [music] and the identity of being the awakened one. What do these seven things have in common? Every single one of them is a way of managing how you are seen. Every one of them is the ego doing what the ego does best, trying to protect you, trying to position [music] you, trying to keep you safe from the terrifying and beautiful vulnerability of just being exactly who you actually are. [music] And the process of letting them go is not a single event. It is not a moment of enlightenment. It is a slow, nonlinear, sometimes frustrating and sometimes deeply moving unwinding. You let go and then you grab back. You release [music] and then you grip again. You get a glimpse of freedom. And then you spend 3 weeks back in the old pattern. This is not failure. [music] This is the actual shape of growth. It is a spiral, not a straight line. Every time you return to an old pattern, you are a little bit less unconscious inside it. Every time you grip again, [music] the grip is a little bit looser. You are circling the same territory, but from a higher elevation each time. And here is what I want to leave you with because I think it is the most important thing of all. The things you are letting go of. The approval seeking, the need to be special, the performance, the certainties, [music] the blame, the bypassing, the spiritual pride. You needed all of them. Every single [music] one. They were not mistakes. They were necessary tools for the stages of life in which you [music] needed them. The approval seeking kept you connected when connection felt essential to survival. The need to be special gave you motivation when motivation was hard to find. [music] The certainties gave you ground to stand on when the ground felt shaky. You do not need to be ashamed of any of it. You needed to live inside those patterns fully, completely without shortcuts before you could genuinely [music] and naturally release them. The releasing is not something you do. It is something that happens when you are ready. [music] When you have genuinely grown past a particular need, you do not have to white knuckle your way to giving it up. It just becomes impossible to maintain. Like trying to believe in Santa Claus at 40 years old, not because you are forcing yourself not to believe, [music] just because you can see too clearly. So if you are in this process right now, if something in this conversation has been landing as recognition rather than information, [music] here is what I want you to hear. You are not losing yourself. You are finding yourself. The version of you that is emerging on the other side of these releases is not a diminished version. It is not a lonier version or a stranger version [music] or a version that no longer belongs anywhere. It is the most genuinely you version that has ever existed. It is the person who was always in there underneath all the performance and the seeking and the managing. And that person, [music] your actual self, does not need to be approved of or seen as special or eternally positive or certain or innocent or transcendent or superior. That person just needs to be here [music] fully here alive in the only life you actually have. [music] That is enough. That is everything. And that is what you are slowly, beautifully, [music] unmistakably becoming.
